items.title: 31.5 Fractional Distillation and Refining of Petroleum

source_refs.note: Topic 31.5 with Figure 31.6 and Quick Check 31.3 (PDF 225-226). The figure's kerosene formula (C10H14) and lubricating-oil range are flagged in a warning. Quick Check answers were derived for the lesson and need review.

blocks.text: Crude oil is a complicated mixture of hydrocarbons that must be separated into simpler, useful hydrocarbons. This is done physically by fractional distillation, which depends on the differences in the boiling points of the hydrocarbons. The crude oil is heated in a furnace until it vaporises, and the vapour passes into a fractionating column, a tall tower in which the temperature falls slowly going up. As the vapour rises, the constituents condense at different heights according to their boiling points: heavier hydrocarbons with higher boiling points condense near the bottom, while lighter hydrocarbons with low boiling points rise further.

blocks.alt: A tall column with trays. Crude oil is heated in a furnace (above 370 C) and the hot vapour enters the base of the column; arrows show the temperature falling to below 20 C at the top and molecules getting smaller going up. Six outlets, top to bottom: gases (LPG) below 25 C; gasoline (petrol) below 40-200 C; kerosene 150-275 C; diesel 250-350 C; lubricating oils 300-370 C; residue (bitumen) above 370 C, each with its uses.
blocks.caption: Fractional distillation of crude oil (original diagram after Figure 31.6).
blocks.long_description: Each fraction is drawn off at the height where the column temperature matches its boiling range. Small molecules with low boiling points leave at the top; the largest molecules stay at the bottom as residue.

blocks.text: Fractional distillation is important because it provides petrochemicals for industrial, domestic and transport purposes.
